ratings.reviewer_notes: Review-level context linking senescence/SASP to regeneration and describing senolytic clearance, but it does not establish a specific senolytic-to-regeneration mechanistic path.
Provides an intermediate link between SASP and wound healing/tissue regeneration, including context-dependent harmful inflammation, but does not test senolytics.
Review discusses senescent-cell clearance and SASP modulation as strategies relevant to tissue repair, but supplies review-level rather than direct experimental evidence.

Direct mouse evidence that dasatinib plus quercetin improves aged muscle regeneration; candidate intermediates include removal of persistent SA-β-Gal+/CD11b+ cells and direct enhancement of myogenic progenitor proliferation.

Direct mechanistic path: dasatinib/quercetin eliminates senescent chondrogenic progenitors, decreases SASP formation, and promotes surviving progenitor proliferation and chondrogenic cartilage regeneration.
Conceptual periodontitis review suggests senescence/SASP can impair stem-cell regeneration and mentions senolytics as a potential strategy, while explicitly noting limited direct evidence.

Human OA cell evidence that ABT-263 selectively removes senescent synovial MSCs, lowers senescence/SASP features, and improves colony formation and chondrogenic capacity relevant to cartilage regeneration.
Direct path in myotonic dystrophy: a BCL-XL senolytic clears senescent myoblasts, reduces SASP expression, restores proliferation and differentiation, and enhances in vivo engraftment/myogenesis.

Mechanistically informative counterpoint: transient SASP exposure induces plasticity, stemness, and regeneration, whereas prolonged exposure causes senescence. Senolytic treatment itself is not tested.

Highly focused review proposing that senolytics remove senescent sources of anti-regenerative secretory factors and thereby restore progenitor function, but the abstract presents synthesis and a proposed mechanism rather than a direct test.
Review supports pathway segments in which stem-cell senescence reduces regeneration and SASP causes inflammation/tissue dysfunction, while discussing senolytic clearance as an intervention.
